title: Moments of Genuine Connection (MGCs) Can Be EXHAUSTING
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Days into his month-long September Invitation focused on tracking MGCs, Stuart names an honest cost of the strategy: it is genuinely exhausting. He leans on David Brooks's How to Know a Person for the deeper justification -- the idea that seeing another person deeply and making them feel seen is a core skill of any healthy person, family, or community, one Brooks argues AI will never be able to replicate. Stuart uses this to reframe MGC fatigue as evidence of real, worthwhile emotional and relational labor rather than a sign something is wrong, quoting psychologist Diana Fosha on resilience growing from being understood by an "attuned, self-possessed other." He estimates the sheer scale of the task -- bringing roughly 133 new students into his mind and heart each year -- and connects the strategy's apparent simplicity to why it's easy to underestimate: teachers rarely receive direct training in it because it seems too basic to teach, even though most people became teachers because someone MGCed with them once. He closes by pointing to a video reflection and hoping it will help fatigued teachers feel seen themselves during the early weeks of school.
points: Stuart names MGC fatigue directly and validates it rather than treating it as a problem to fix, framing it instead as proof of genuine emotional and relational labor.
He grounds the strategy's importance in David Brooks's claim that seeing someone deeply is one thing AI will never be able to do, positioning MGCs as an irreplaceably human skill in an AI era.
The scale point -- roughly 133 new students to hold in mind and heart each year -- makes the abstract idea of teacher burnout risk concrete and numerically grounded.

His closing move reframes the strategy's apparent simplicity as a trap: "just because something appears simple does not mean it is easy," which is why MGCs don't get taught explicitly even though most teachers became teachers because someone did it for them.
quotes: There is one skill that lies at the heart of any healthy person, family, school, community organization, or society: the ability to see someone else deeply and make them feel seen—to accurately know another person, to let them feel valued, heard, and understood.

Artificial intelligence is going to do many things for us in the decades ahead, and replace humans at many tasks, but one thing it will never be able to do is create person-to-person connections. If you want to thrive in the age of AI, you better become exceptionally good at connecting with others.
Seeing a student and then communicating that sight to students is a "skill"; it's "a powerfully creative act;" it involves the beaming of the light of my attention on a student.

Do you know how much work it takes to bring 133 new students into my mind and heart? To have them exist in my inner world, to attune myself to them, and to maintain a sense of self-possession as I do so? A LOT!

Most of us became teachers because we had a teacher or two who successfully MGCed with us. And much of the rest became teachers because they didn't receive enough of this stuff and wanted to make a change for future students.
But just because something appears simple does not mean it is easy. I'm telling you: this is work.
